title: Ibadah
def: Worship and devotion to God, in ritual and in the whole of a life lived for Him.
what: The Quran says: “I did not create jinn and humans except to worship Me” (51:56). The five pillars are its core acts, but the Prophet taught that every good deed done for God’s sake is worship, even a kind word or removing harm from the road (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim). Prayer, fasting, charity and pilgrimage are called ibadat in law, as distinct from dealings between people.

title: Iblis
def: The devil, who refused to prostrate to Adam and now tempts humanity; in the Quran he is one of the jinn, not an angel.
what: The Quran says Iblis refused to prostrate to Adam, saying “I am better than him: You created me of fire and him of clay” (7:12). He asked for respite until the Day of Judgement and vowed to lead people astray, though “you have no authority over My servants” (7:14–18, 15:42). He is “one of the jinn” (18:50) and not an angel. “The Devil” and “devils” (shayāṭīn) also refer to evil beings who whisper to people (114:4–6).
misread: That Islam teaches Satan is an angel who rebelled, as in some Christian tradition.
sources: The Quran says that angels “do not disobey God in what He commands them” (66:6), so Iblis, who disobeyed, is not one of them. The Prophet taught believers to seek refuge from Satan and said that he flows in the human being like blood (Sahih al-Bukhari); the remedy is the remembrance of God.

title: Ibn Abbas
def: A cousin of the Prophet (d. around 687) who became one of the great early scholars of Quranic interpretation.
what: Abdullah ibn Abbas was born in Mecca about three years before the Hijra and was a boy when the Prophet died. He asked the older Companions about the Quran and its background, and was called “the interpreter of the Quran”. It is reported that the Prophet prayed: “O God, give him understanding of the religion” (Sahih al-Bukhari). He died in Taif.
sources: Much commentary is attributed to him, and scholars sort reports by their chain of narrators: some are firmly established and some are doubtful, so later works that bear his name are not all his.

title: Ibn Ishaq
def: The earliest major biographer of the Prophet (d. around 767), whose work survives mainly in Ibn Hisham’s edition.
what: Muhammad ibn Ishaq, born in Medina, collected traditions about the life of the Prophet, his battles and the earlier prophets, and wrote them as a continuous narrative. His book survives through the edition of Ibn Hisham (d. around 833) and in quotations by al-Tabari. It is the basis of almost every later biography.
sources: Sira is not held to the same standard as hadith of law. Scholars praised Ibn Ishaq on the campaigns but some, such as Malik, criticised him, and later writers weigh his reports against the Quran and hadith collections.

title: Ibn Umm Maktum
def: A blind Companion of the Prophet who served as a muezzin and as his deputy in Medina.
what: Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, a relative of Khadija, was early to accept Islam. He gave the call to prayer in Medina alongside Bilal, and it is reported that the Prophet left him in charge of Medina when he went on expeditions. Surah 80, ‘Abasa, is traditionally linked to him: it begins with a rebuke that the Prophet turned from the blind man who came to him while he was speaking to the leaders of Quraysh.
sources: The Quran presents the correction without softening it, and the Prophet is reported to have honoured Ibn Umm Maktum afterwards. Scholars have taken it as a sign that revelation is not the Prophet’s own composition, and as a lesson that the poor and disabled come first.

title: Ibrahim ibn Muhammad
def: The infant son of the Prophet and Mariya, who died at about eighteen months.
what: Ibrahim was born in Medina in 8 AH to Mariya al-Qibtiyya. When he died the Prophet wept, and said: “The eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, but we say only what pleases our Lord. O Ibrahim, we are grieved at your parting” (Sahih al-Bukhari). He was told that Ibrahim would have a nurse in Paradise to complete his nursing (Sahih Muslim).
misread: A solar eclipse occurred on the day of his death, and some people said it was for his sake. The Prophet answered that the sun and moon are signs of God and do not eclipse for anyone’s death or life (Sahih al-Bukhari), and so refused a cheap miracle at his moment of grief.

title: Idda
def: The waiting period a woman observes after divorce or the death of her husband.
what: A divorced woman waits three monthly cycles (2:228), a widow four months and ten days (2:234), and a pregnant woman until she delivers (65:4). The wisdom is to be sure of paternity, to give husband and wife time to reconcile, and for a widow to mourn. During it the husband must provide for a divorced wife and not force her out (65:1, 65:6).

title: Idris
def: A prophet the Quran describes as truthful and raised to a high station.
what: “Mention in the Book Idris; he was a man of truth, a prophet, and We raised him to a high place” (19:56–57). He is also named among the patient (21:85). The Quran does not give his story or say where he lived; many commentators identified him with Enoch, whom the Bible says “God took”, and others differed.

title: Ihram
def: The state of consecration entered for the pilgrimage, with its simple dress and restrictions.
what: A pilgrim enters ihram at a set place with the intention for Hajj or Umrah. Men wear two unsewn white cloths and women their normal modest dress; all avoid perfume, cutting hair or nails, hunting, marital relations and quarrelling (2:196–197, 5:95). The equal dress removes marks of rank so that the rich and poor stand alike before God.

title: Ihsan
def: Excellence in faith and conduct: to worship God as though you see Him.
what: In the hadith of Gabriel, the Prophet defines iḥsān as worshipping God as though you see Him, for if you do not see Him, He sees you (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). The Quran says God commands justice and ihsan (16:90), and asks: “Is the reward for ihsan anything but ihsan?” (55:60).
misread: That Islam is mostly rules and legal duties.
sources: The hadith of Gabriel sets out three levels: islām, the acts of worship; īmān, belief; and iḥsān, the inward excellence behind both. The long tradition of Muslim spiritual writing, from al-Ghazali to Rumi, grew around this third level.

title: Ijma
def: Consensus of the scholars of a period on a ruling; one of the sources of Islamic law.
what: The Sunni schools take four sources of law: the Quran, the Sunnah, ijmāʿ and analogy (qiyās). Consensus means agreement among qualified scholars of an age on a point of law. The Prophet is reported to have said that his community will not agree on error (Ibn Majah, graded hasan by some), and the idea is also argued from the Quran (4:115).
sources: Scholars have debated whether it can truly be known, and the schools differ on its scope. A few matters, such as the five daily prayers, are accepted by all Muslims.

title: Ijtihad
def: Scholarly effort to reach a ruling from the sources, when the text does not state it plainly.
what: The Prophet said: “When a judge exercises ijtihad and is right he has two rewards, and if he errs he has one” (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). A scholar qualified in Arabic, the Quran, hadith and the principles of law is called a mujtahid. Ijtihad is how the law meets new cases, from medicine to finance, within the limits of the text and consensus.
sources: The old claim that “the gate of ijtihad was closed” is rejected by many historians, who show that jurists went on giving fresh rulings, and by modern scholars who ask for it to be used more freely.

title: Illiyin
def: The high register in which the deeds of the righteous are recorded.
what: “Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ‘Illiyyun. And what will make you know what ‘Illiyyun is? A written record, witnessed by those brought near” (83:18–21). It contrasts with Sijjin, the register of the wicked (83:7–9).

title: Images and depiction
def: Why many Muslims avoid images of the Prophet, and why the Danish cartoons of 2005–06 caused such anger.
what: Islamic tradition discourages depicting prophets and worshipping images, as a safeguard against idolatry. Many hadith warn against picture-makers (Sahih al-Bukhari). Pictures of the Prophet were nonetheless painted in some Persian and Ottoman manuscripts, with the face veiled or left blank in later periods. In 2005 a Danish newspaper printed cartoons mocking the Prophet and there were protests in many countries, some violent.
misread: That Islam demands violence in answer to insult.
sources: The Quran says to leave those who mock (4:140, 6:68), and the Prophet bore insults with patience. Many Muslim scholars and organisations condemned the violent reaction, which they said did more harm to the Prophet’s reputation than the cartoons.

title: Imam
def: A leader: the one who leads prayer, and a title of respected scholars.
what: In every mosque the imam leads the congregation, and the Prophet said: “The imam is appointed to be followed” (Sahih al-Bukhari). The title is also given to great scholars, such as Imam Abu Hanifa or Imam al-Shafi‘i.

title: Iman
def: Faith: belief in God, His angels, scriptures and messengers, the Last Day and the decree, which the Quran joins with righteous deeds.
what: “The righteous man is he who believes in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Book and the prophets” (2:177). The Quran adds works: “those who believe and do righteous deeds” appears dozens of times. It describes the believers as those whose hearts tremble when God is mentioned and whose faith grows when His verses are recited (8:2–4). It distinguishes outward submission (islām) from faith (īmān) in the heart (49:14).
sources: The Quran asks Muslims to believe in all revelations: “we make no distinction between any of His messengers” (2:285). That includes the earlier scriptures, and the Quran tells the Prophet that if he doubts, he should ask those who have been reading the Book before him (10:94).

title: Immaculate conception
def: The Quran says that Mary was protected from Satan at her birth, and that Jesus was born miraculously without a father.
what: Mary’s mother prayed: “I seek refuge for her and her offspring in You from the accursed Satan” (3:36). The Prophet said that every child is touched by Satan at birth, except Mary and her son (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). The Quran says that God breathed His spirit into Mary (66:12), and that Jesus was created by God’s word as Adam was created without parents (3:45–47, 3:59).
misread: Islam has no doctrine of original sin, so there is nothing to be “immaculate” from in the Christian sense. The Muslim teaching is of protection, and of miraculous birth, from a God who creates as He wills.

title: Imran
def: The name of the family of Mary, whom the Quran says God chose, and after which the third surah is named.
what: “God chose Adam and Noah, the family of Abraham and the family of Imran over all peoples” (3:33). The wife of Imran made a vow for what was in her womb (3:35), and Mary is called “daughter of Imran” (66:12).
misread: Mary is called “sister of Aaron” (19:28). The Prophet explained that the people of earlier times were named after the righteous before them (Sahih Muslim). Muslim scholars hold that it does not mean she was the sister of Moses’ brother, and the Imran here is not the father of Moses.

title: Imru al-Qais
def: A prince of the Kinda tribe in the sixth century, usually reckoned the greatest of the pre-Islamic poets.
what: His ode, one of the Mu‘allaqat, begins with the famous lines about stopping to weep at an abandoned camp, and it is a model of Arabic poetry before the Quran. The Quran came to a people proud of their eloquence, and challenged them to produce a surah like it (2:23). It is the reason that the Arabic poetry of the age is studied closely in Quranic interpretation.

title: Inheritance
def: The Quran sets fixed shares for family heirs and allows a bequest of up to a third.
what: The Quran fixes shares for children, parents, spouses and siblings (4:11–12, 4:176). A son receives twice the share of a daughter, but each parent receives a sixth, and the mother and father may receive equal shares. A person can leave a bequest of up to one third of his estate to others, as the Prophet told Sa’d ibn Abi Waqqas (Sahih al-Bukhari).
misread: That Islam values a woman as half a man.
sources: The reason usually given for the difference in the son’s share is that the male is required to support the household, to pay the dowry and to maintain his wife and children, while a woman’s inheritance, dowry and earnings are hers alone and she is under no obligation to spend them. The Quran gave women a right to inherit at a time when in many societies they did not (4:7).

title: Injil
def: The Gospel: the revelation God gave to Jesus, which the Quran says confirmed the Torah.
what: The Quran says God gave Jesus the Gospel, “in it guidance and light, confirming the Torah” (5:46), and tells “the people of the Gospel” to judge by what God revealed in it (5:47). Muslims understand the Injīl as the message revealed to Jesus himself, not as the four Gospels, which are accounts about him by his followers.
misread: That Muslims have no use for the Gospels, or say they simply contradict the Quran.
sources: Muslim scholars through the centuries have quoted the Gospels, for instance on the sayings of Jesus, and many see in them a record that carries much true teaching. They differ with the Christian view on the cross and on Jesus’ nature. The question of what became of the original Gospel is taken up in the article linked here.

title: Intercession
def: Pleading on someone’s behalf before God, which is possible only by God’s permission.
what: “Who is there that can intercede with Him except by His permission?” (2:255); “Intercession belongs wholly to God” (39:44). Yet the Prophet said he will be given the right of intercession on the Day of Judgement, and will fall in prostration before God before it is allowed (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim). It is for the believers who are in need of mercy, according to the majority.
misread: Some Muslims, in popular devotion, call on saints to intercede. Others regard calling on anyone but God as shirk, and teach that one asks God directly, since He is near (2:186). This is a disagreement within the community, and not between Islam and its critics.

title: Intoxicants
def: The Quran prohibits intoxicants in stages, and calls them “an abomination of Satan’s handiwork” (5:90).
what: The first verse says “in them is great sin and some benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit” (2:219). The second says “do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated” (4:43). The last says: “Intoxicants, gambling, idols and divining arrows are an abomination of Satan’s work; avoid it” (5:90–91). The Prophet said “every intoxicant is khamr, and every khamr is forbidden” (Sahih Muslim), which scholars extend to drugs.
misread: That the Quran promises wine in Paradise, so it contradicts its own ban.
sources: The wine of Paradise is described as different: “no headache nor intoxication from it” (37:47, 56:19). Muslim scholars explain that what is forbidden here is the harm of the drink, and it is promised there without harm.

title: Iram
def: A place named in the Quran as the home of the ancient people of ‘Ad, “of the pillars”.
what: “Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with ‘Ad, Iram of the pillars, the like of which was not created in the land?” (89:6–8). The people of ‘Ad were warned by the prophet Hud and were destroyed by a violent wind (7:65–72, 69:6–8).
sources: Commentators differed whether Iram is a tribe, a city or an ancestor. Claims that the lost city of Ubar has been found are not established, and the Quran’s lesson is the fall of the proud, which does not depend on the location.

title: Iron
def: The Quran says God “sent down” iron, and gives it the title of the fifty-seventh surah.
what: “We sent down iron, in which is great strength and benefits for people” (57:25). Iron is also the metal of the barrier that Dhu al-Qarnayn built (18:96) and of David’s mail (34:10–11).
misread: Some modern writers say “sent down” means that iron fell from space. The same verb is used in the Quran for livestock (39:6) and clothing (7:26), and Arabic usage means “provided”, so scholars do not rest an argument on it.

title: Isa
def: Jesus, son of Mary: the Messiah and a mighty messenger of God in Islam.
what: The Quran calls him the Messiah, “honoured in this world and the next” (3:45), and says he was born of the virgin Mary (3:47, 19:16–21), spoke as an infant (19:30–33), and, by God’s leave, healed the sick, raised the dead and gave life to clay birds (3:49, 5:110). It names him “a Word from God” and “a spirit from Him” (4:171).
Muslims love and honour him, and believe he will return before the end of time (Sahih al-Bukhari).
misread: That Islam denies or insults Jesus.
sources: The Quran does not accept that he is God or God’s son (5:72–75, 5:116–117), and says that his creation was like Adam’s, from dust (3:59). The disagreement is about what Jesus said of himself, and about the crucifixion (4:157). Both are taken up in the articles linked here.

title: Isaac
def: Son of Abraham and Sarah and father of Jacob, named as a prophet in the Quran.
what: Angels gave Abraham and his wife the good news of Isaac, and of Jacob after him, when she was old (11:71–73; 37:112). “We gave him Isaac and Jacob, each of whom We guided” (6:84). Isaac is among those whom God made leaders who guide by His command (21:72–73).
sources: The Quran does not name the son whom Abraham was told to sacrifice (37:99–113). Some early scholars said it was Isaac and many others, including most later commentators, said Ishmael. Muslims believe the Quran leaves it open on purpose, and the lesson of submission is the same.

title: Ishmael
def: Son of Abraham and Hagar, a prophet and messenger who helped his father raise the Kaaba.
what: “Mention in the Book Ishmael; he was true to his promise, and was a messenger and a prophet” (19:54). Abraham and Ishmael raised the foundations of the House, praying: “Our Lord, accept it from us” (2:127). According to a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, Hagar ran between Safa and Marwa seeking water for her infant son, and Zamzam sprang up; the rite of sa‘i at Hajj recalls her.
sources: The tradition that the Arabs descend from Ishmael is a matter of genealogy that the Quran does not state, and scholars differ over the details.

title: Islam
def: Submission to God, the name the Quran gives to the religion of all the prophets.
what: The word comes from the root s-l-m, which means submission and also peace and wholeness. “The religion with God is Islam” (3:19), and “Today I have perfected your religion for you, completed My favour on you and approved Islam as your religion” (5:3). Abraham “was neither Jew nor Christian but a Muslim, upright” (3:67), and Muslims call each prophet’s message by the same name. In the hadith of Gabriel Islam is the five pillars, as faith is the six articles and ihsan is worshipping God as if one sees Him (Sahih Muslim).

title: Islamic finance
def: Banking and investment that avoid interest (ribā) and speculation, using profit-sharing, sale and leasing instead.
what: Islamic finance uses contracts such as muḍāraba (profit-sharing), murābaḥa (sale at an agreed mark-up), ijāra (leasing) and ṣukūk (asset-backed certificates). It has grown since the 1970s, and Islamic banks now operate in many countries, with Muslim and non-Muslim customers.
sources: Critics say that some products only imitate conventional loans, and Muslim economists have said the same. The aim in the law is to tie profit to risk and to real assets.

title: Islamophobia
def: Prejudice, hostility or discrimination against Muslims because of their faith.
what: Many governments and rights bodies use the word for hatred of Muslims, and records show attacks on mosques and on people in Europe and North America. Criticising a belief is different from hating the people who hold it, and Muslims welcome an honest discussion of their religion. The Quran says: “Do not let hatred of a people make you unjust; be just, that is closer to piety” (5:8), and teaches kindness to those who do not fight Muslims over religion (60:8).
sources: The word is disputed: some use it to shield ideas from criticism, others say that this misses the real harm to ordinary people. This entry takes the second sense, and welcomes the first kind of discussion.

title: Ismah
def: The belief that God protected the prophets from major sin and from error in conveying His message.
what: Muslim scholars hold that prophets are preserved from lying, from hiding the message and from grave sins. The Quran speaks openly of their lapses: Adam’s slip (20:121), Moses striking a man (28:15–16), David’s test (38:24) and the Prophet’s frown at the blind man (80:1). Each is followed by repentance and forgiveness. They show that prophets are human, and teach how to return to God.

title: Isnad
def: The chain of narrators by which a report is traced back to its source.
what: “The chain is part of the religion,” said Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak, “and without the chain anyone could say what he liked” (quoted in the introduction to Sahih Muslim). Ibn Sirin said that at first people did not ask about chains, but after the civil strife of the first century they said, “Name your men.”
This produced a large literature on the narrators: who they were, where they lived, whom they met, how good their memory was and whether they were honest.
misread: That Muslims accepted reports without any checking.
sources: Whatever one concludes about the method, it was a deliberate attempt to test reports by their sources, and it was applied to the most revered figures as well as to unknowns. A report might be rejected because one narrator in the chain was unreliable, however attractive its content.

title: Isra and Miraj
def: The Prophet’s night journey from Mecca to Jerusalem and his ascent through the heavens, reported in the Quran and in hadith.
what: The Quran begins chapter 17: “Glory to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, whose surroundings We have blessed” (17:1). Chapter 53 describes his seeing “at the Lote Tree of the Boundary” (53:13–18). The hadith, such as the long report in Sahih al-Bukhari, add the ascent through the seven heavens and the prayers being fixed at five a day.
misread: That there was no “Farthest Mosque” (al-Aqsa) in Jerusalem in the Prophet’s time.
sources: Masjid means a place of prostration, not a building. The Farthest Mosque is the sacred precinct in Jerusalem where the Temple had stood, which the Prophet’s contemporaries knew as Bayt al-Maqdis. The buildings now called al-Aqsa and the Dome of the Rock were built later. The Quran’s verse names the place, not a building.

title: Israel
def: The Quranic name of the prophet Jacob, and of his descendants, the Children of Israel.
what: “All food was lawful to the Children of Israel except what Israel made unlawful for himself” (3:93), where Israel is Jacob. The Quran tells of their rescue from Pharaoh (2:49–50), of favour shown them above the peoples of their time (2:47, 45:16), and also of their disobedience (5:78). It praises the faithful among them (7:159, 3:113–114).
misread: The Quranic term is for a people of the past and in Jewish scripture; it does not name the modern state. Its criticisms of some people’s actions, as of Muslims’ own, are about conduct and not about blood.

title: Istighfar
def: Asking God’s forgiveness, which the Quran urges and links with blessing and relief.
what: “Seek forgiveness from your Lord; He is ever Forgiving; He will send down rain upon you in abundance” (71:10–11). The Prophet is reported to have sought God’s forgiveness more than seventy times a day (Sahih al-Bukhari). “Astaghfir Allah” is said after the prayer.

title: Itikaf
def: Spending days in the mosque in devotion, especially in the last ten days of Ramadan.
what: The Quran mentions staying in the mosques in worship (2:187). Aisha reported that the Prophet used to do itikaf in the last ten days of Ramadan until God took his soul, and that his wives did it after him (Sahih al-Bukhari). The one who does it leaves the mosque only for need, and spends the time in prayer, Quran and remembrance, hoping for the Night of Power.

title: 'Id Mubarak
ar: عيد مبارك / كل عام وأنتم بخير
tr: ʿĪd Mubārak; Kull ʿām wa-antum bi-khayr
def: “Blessed feast; may you be well every year”: the greeting said at ʿĪd al-Fiṭr, ʿĪd al-Aḍḥā and other annual celebrations.
what: ʿĪd Mubārak means “a blessed festival”. Kull ʿām wa-antum bi-khayr means “every year, may you be well”, a wish that the person will see the day again in good health and happiness. Muslims say the two together, or either alone, to family, friends and neighbours on the mornings of ʿĪd al-Fiṭr, which ends Ramadan, and ʿĪd al-Aḍḥā, which falls at the end of the pilgrimage rites. People also use the greeting at weddings, anniversaries and other yearly celebrations. It is a custom of courtesy and goodwill and does not come from a text of the Quran. Many Muslims also add a prayer, such as asking God to accept their fasting or worship.
misread: Non-Muslims sometimes think it is a prayer formula with a fixed ritual setting, while it is an ordinary greeting that anyone may use.

faruqi.term: ‘ĪD MUBĀRAK. KULL ‘ĀM WA ANTUM BI KHAYR.

title: I'jaz al-Qur'an
def: The inimitability of the Quran: the claim that no one can produce its like, which shows its divine origin.
what: Iʿjāz means making others unable to match something. Iʿjāz al-Qurʾān is the doctrine that the Quran cannot be equalled in its language, meaning and effect, and that this is evidence of its divine origin. The Quran itself issues the challenge to produce a surah like it (2:23, 10:38), and to bring ten (11:13) or even the whole of it (17:88), even if humans and jinn united to try.

Muslims have found the inimitability in the Quran’s Arabic style and rhythm, its structure, its knowledge of the unseen and its effect on listeners. Scholars such as al-Baqillani and al-Jurjani wrote on its eloquence. Faruqi stresses that the Quran is the verbatim word of God, and on this view its form cannot be separated from its meaning, which is why translation never reproduces it fully.
misread: It is mistaken for a claim that the Quran is simply beautiful poetry, while the claim is that the whole work cannot be matched by any human effort.
sources: Scholars differ on the grounds of inimitability: some stress eloquence, others the content, others that God withheld the ability to imitate. All agree that the challenge was never met.

title: Ijma', al-
def: Consensus: the agreement of qualified scholars on a ruling, accepted as a source of Islamic law after the Quran and Sunna.
what: Ijmāʿ means agreement. In Islamic law it names the agreement of the qualified jurists of a given age on a legal question, and the schools count it among the sources of law after the Quran and the Sunna. Once such agreement is established, later scholars treat the ruling as settled. Jurists base the authority of consensus on texts such as 4:115, which warns against following a path other than that of the believers, and on a saying reported in several forms that the Prophet’s community will not agree on an error. Faruqi counts it with the sources from which Islamic law is derived.
misread: Some picture it as a vote of the general public or a majority decision, but it refers to the agreement of those qualified to give legal rulings.
sources: Scholars disagree about who counts for consensus, whether it extends beyond the Companions, and whether it can be known to have taken place. Some, such as Ahmad ibn Hanbal, were cautious about claiming it.

title: Ijma' al-Sarih, al-
def: Explicit consensus: agreement of the jurists stated openly, each by word or act, on a legal question.
what: Al-ijmāʿ al-ṣarīḥ is the clearly expressed form of consensus. The word ṣarīḥ means plain or explicit. Here every jurist of the age states his view on a question, whether in speech or by deed, and the statements all agree. Jurists treat this as the strongest kind of consensus, and they contrast it with silent agreement (al-ijmāʿ al-sukūtī). Since the agreement is declared, the schools generally accept it as proof for a ruling, while they disagree among themselves about how often it has actually occurred.

title: Ijma' al-Sukuti, al-
def: Tacit consensus: one or more jurists give a ruling and the others, aware of it, raise no objection.
what: Al-ijmāʿ al-sukūtī means silent consensus. It arises when a jurist or several jurists derive a ruling from a source and the other jurists of the age know of it and do not object, so their silence is read as acceptance. Faruqi defines it by the jurists’ not objecting to the derivation of a given prescription from a source. Schools differ on its weight. Some, including many Hanafi scholars, accept it as a proof, with conditions, while others, among them many Shafiʿi scholars, hold that silence alone cannot establish agreement. It is the weaker of the two kinds, set against express consensus (al-ijmāʿ al-ṣarīḥ).

title: Ijtihad, al-
def: Independent reasoning by a qualified scholar to derive rulings from the Quran, the Sunna and the other legitimate sources.
what: Ijtihād comes from the root j-h-d, meaning to exert effort, and it names the exertion of a qualified jurist to reach a ruling on a matter that the sources do not settle directly. Faruqi calls it creative self-exertion to derive laws from the legitimate sources. It works with the Quran, the Sunna, consensus and analogy, and the person doing it is called a mujtahid. A well-known hadith says that a judge who exerts himself and judges correctly has two rewards, and one who errs has one (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim). The saying shows that sincere effort is valued even when the result is mistaken.
misread: It is mistaken for private opinion or freedom to reinterpret the religion at will, but it is a disciplined method that only trained scholars may use.
sources: Scholars set conditions for the mujtahid: knowledge of Arabic, the Quran, hadith and the principles of jurisprudence. A long-running debate asks whether the “gate” of ijtihad closed in later centuries, and many modern scholars say that it did not.

title: Ikhlas
def: Sincerity: pure devotion to God, with firm conviction and loyalty to Him and commitment to His will.
what: Ikhlāṣ means purifying one’s religion and one’s deeds for God alone. The Quran commands: “They were commanded only to worship God, being sincere to Him in religion” (98:5; also 39:2). It is the inner side of worship, joined to firm belief, faithfulness to God and the resolve to do what He wills. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim says that deeds are judged by their intentions, and scholars cite it on the place of sincerity in every act. Surah 112, which declares God’s oneness, is called Surat al-Ikhlāṣ, and the sincerity of faith is understood as the opposite of showing off (riyāʾ) and of associating partners with God.
misread: It is rendered “sincerity” only, though in Islam it means directing the whole intention to God, not simply being honest about one’s feelings.

title: 'Ilal al-Hadith
def: The science of hidden defects in hadith: flaws in a report that look sound on the surface but weaken it.
what: ʿIlal is the plural of ʿilla, here a hidden defect. The science of ʿilal al-ḥadīth studies the qualities or circumstances that may weaken a report that otherwise seems sound. Examples include a break in a chain that is not apparent, a narrator who attributed to the Prophet (peace be upon him) the words of a Companion, or a mix-up of two chains. It is regarded as one of the most demanding branches of hadith criticism, since spotting such defects needs wide knowledge of narrators and their reports. Early critics such as Ali ibn al-Madini worked in it, and Ibn Abi Hatim al-Razi (d. 938) wrote a well-known work on the subject.

title: ʿIlm, al-
def: Knowledge of the patterns God has set in creation, in nature, in the person and in society, reached through the senses, intuition and reason.
what: ʿIlm means knowledge, and the Quran gives it great honour: “Are those who know equal to those who do not know?” (39:9). Faruqi defines it as knowledge of the patterns of God in creation. These patterns are found in nature, which the natural and exact sciences study, in the personal realm, which the humanities study, and in society, which the social sciences study. The patterns can be known through the senses, through intuition, theoretical and practical, and through reason. The Quran also commands the prayer, “My Lord, increase me in knowledge” (20:114). On this view, to study creation is to study the signs of God, and no real conflict exists between faith and the pursuit of knowledge.
misread: It is often limited to religious learning, though the word covers every field in which the patterns of creation are studied.
sources: The Quran says that those who truly fear God among His servants are the people of knowledge (35:28). Muslim scholars of the classical period carried the word into medicine, astronomy, mathematics and other fields.

title: 'Immah
def: The turban, a head-covering worn by many Muslim men and by some scholars as a mark of their calling.
what: ʿImāmah is the turban, a cloth wound around the head. Faruqi lists it among the garments of Muslim dress as a head-covering. The Prophet (peace be upon him) is reported to have worn a black turban when he entered Mecca (Sahih Muslim), and many Muslims, especially scholars, wear it for the sake of that example. It is not an obligation of the faith. Colours, styles and the way it is wound differ widely between regions, from the Arabian peninsula to South Asia and West Africa. In many places a turban marks a scholar, a pilgrim or a person of standing, and in others it is worn only on special occasions.
misread: It is often assumed to be a required religious uniform, but it is a customary garment that carries a sunna-inspired meaning for some.

title: In Sha'a Allah
def: “If God wills”: said whenever one speaks of the future, in acknowledgement that outcomes rest with God.
what: In shāʾ Allāh means “if God wills”. Muslims say it whenever they speak of something they intend to do, and they say it as an acknowledgement that no plan comes to pass unless God allows it. The Quran teaches it directly: “Never say of anything, ‘I will do that tomorrow,’ without adding, ‘if God wills’” (18:23–24). Examples of the phrase appear in the Quran in the speech of prophets, as when Ishmael tells his father that he will find him patient “if God wills” (37:102). People use the phrase when making promises, arranging meetings and stating hopes. It reminds the speaker that his own effort is real but depends on God’s decree.
misread: It is often taken as a polite way of saying “maybe” or “probably not”, while the phrase expresses the speaker’s intention together with trust in God.

title: Inna Allah wa Mala'ikatahu Yusalluna 'ala al-Nabiyy
ar: إن الله وملائكته يصلون على النبي. يا أيها الذين آمنوا صلوا عليه وسلموا تسليما
tr: Inna Allāha wa-malāʾikatahu yuṣallūna ʿalā al-nabiyy; yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū ṣallū ʿalayhi wa-sallimū taslīmā
def: “God and His angels bless the Prophet; O believers, invoke blessings and peace upon him”: the verse recited in the Friday sermon.
what: These words are the Quran’s verse 33:56. They state that God and His angels bless the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and call on the believers to ask for blessings and peace on him. The imam recites the verse in the khuṭba, the Friday sermon, and the congregation answers quietly with the proper invocation, such as “May God bless him and grant him peace”. The verse is the basis for the practice of invoking blessings on the Prophet whenever his name is spoken or heard. Scholars teach that the invocation expresses love and gratitude toward the messenger through whom the Quran came. In the daily prayer, Muslims also recite the blessings in the closing sitting.
misread: The invocation is sometimes mistaken for worship of the Prophet, but the verse asks for God’s blessings on him and so keeps all worship for God.
sources: The Prophet is reported to have said that whoever invokes a blessing on him once, God will bless that person tenfold (Sahih Muslim).

faruqi.term: INNA ALLAH WA MALĀ’IKATAHU YUṢALLŪNA ‘ALĀ AL NABIYY. YĀ AYYUHA ALLADHĪNA ĀMANŪ ṢALLŪ ‘ALAYHI WA SALLIMŪ TASLĪMAN.

title: Inna Lillahi wa Inna Ilayhi Raji'un
def: “We belong to God and to Him we shall return”: said on meeting loss, grief or the news of a death.
what: This phrase comes from the Quran (2:156), which describes those who are patient as the ones “who, when affliction strikes them, say: ‘We belong to God, and to Him we shall return.’” Muslims say it on hearing of a death, and on any loss, tragedy or sorrow. It affirms that life, health and possessions all belong to God, and that every person will return to Him. The saying is reported in Sahih Muslim, in the account of Umm Salama, that the Prophet (peace be upon him) taught it together with a prayer: “O God, reward me in my affliction and give me something better in its place.” People often say it at funerals and when they offer condolences.
misread: Observers sometimes see it as a statement of resignation, whereas it is a statement of trust in God and an expression of patience.

faruqi.term: INNĀ LILLAHI WA INNĀ ILAYHI RĀJI‘ŪN.

title: Inni Da'in fa Amminu
def: “I am about to supplicate, so say Amin”: the imam’s call for the congregation to join his prayer.
what: The words mean “I am a supplicant, so say Āmīn.” The imam says them at the end of the sermon or after the prayer, before reciting supplications, to ask those who are present to join him by saying Āmīn after each invocation. Āmīn means “may it be so” or “answer, O God”. The phrase belongs to the customs of the Friday sermon and congregational prayer, and the text does not come from the Quran or a fixed hadith. Muslims find a basis for the practice in the value that their tradition gives to supplication together, and in the Prophet’s example of saying Āmīn after reciting al-Fātiḥa. Practice differs by region.

title: Iqamah
def: The second call, given just before a congregational prayer begins; from the root meaning to establish.
what: Iqāmah comes from aqāma, meaning to set up or establish. Faruqi defines it as the beginning of ṣalāh or of any other ritual of worship. In practice the word names the call said inside the mosque just before a congregational prayer starts, in words close to those of the adhān, with the addition of qad qāmat al-ṣalāh, “the prayer has begun”. The congregation stands in rows after the call and the imam begins. The related Quranic phrase aqīmū al-ṣalāh (2:43) means to establish the prayer, which is to perform it fully and regularly. The term thus links the call with the larger idea of keeping the ritual of worship in being.
misread: It is sometimes called a second adhan, as if it only repeated the first, whereas it announces that the prayer itself is starting.

title: Isra', al-
def: The Prophet’s night journey from Mecca to Jerusalem, and back to Mecca, named in Quran 17:1.
what: Al-Isrāʾ is the night journey of Muhammad (peace be upon him) from Mecca to Jerusalem (al-Quds) and back. The Quran begins surah 17: “Glory to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, around which We have blessed” (17:1). The surah takes its name from this event, which the tradition places in the later Meccan years.

Hadith accounts add that the Prophet then ascended through the heavens, an event called the miʿrāj, and that the daily prayers were prescribed on that occasion (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim). Many Muslims commemorate the night with prayer. Scholars hold different views on whether the journey was of the body and spirit together, though most take it as a physical and spiritual journey.
sources: The verse names no date and no details beyond the two mosques, so the story of the night comes from the hadith literature.

title: Istad'afa
def: To exploit the weak or to impose domination over them; the act of the oppressor toward the vulnerable.
what: Istaḍʿafa means to treat someone as weak and so to exploit or dominate him. The Quran uses the verb for Pharaoh, who “oppressed a group of them, killing their sons and sparing their women” (28:4). The passive form describes the victims, “those who were oppressed in the land” (28:5), whom God promises to favour. The related word mustaḍʿafūn, the oppressed, appears in 4:75, where believers are urged to fight for the oppressed men, women and children who cry out for a protector. Faruqi includes the verb among the key terms because it names a basic wrong: to take advantage of the helplessness of others or to impose imperial rule over them.

title: Istaghfara
def: To seek God’s forgiveness by asking Him to cover and pardon one’s sins.
what: Istaghfara means to ask for forgiveness (maghfira), and in Islamic usage to ask God to pardon one’s sins. The Quran presents it as a path open to all: “Seek forgiveness of your Lord; He is ever Forgiving” (71:10), and it describes the God-conscious as those who remember God and seek forgiveness for their sins when they err (3:135). Muslims say astaghfir Allāh, “I seek God’s forgiveness”, after prayers and in daily life. The Prophet (peace be upon him) himself sought forgiveness more than seventy times a day, according to Sahih al-Bukhari, which shows that the practice is for the best of people and not only for sinners. The noun is istighfār.

title: Istakbara
def: To be arrogant by falsely supposing oneself greater than others, and above God’s command.
what: Istakbara means to consider oneself great and to behave accordingly. Faruqi defines it as falsely assuming that one is the greater. The Quran uses the verb of Iblis, who refused to bow to Adam: “He refused and was arrogant, and he was one of the unbelievers” (2:34). It uses it also for Pharaoh and his hosts, who “were arrogant in the land without right” (28:39). The Quran treats arrogance as a root of rejecting the truth, because it keeps a person from accepting guidance. The related noun istikbār names the condition. In Islamic teaching only God is truly great (al-Kabīr), and anyone who claims greatness for himself takes a position that belongs to God alone.
sources: A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that no one with an atom’s weight of arrogance in his heart will enter paradise.

title: Istawu Yarhamukum Allah
def: “Straighten your rows; may God have mercy on you”: the imam’s call to the congregation before the prayer begins.
what: The words mean “Straighten yourselves; may God show you mercy.” The imam says them to the congregation before the prayer so that the worshippers stand in straight rows, shoulder to shoulder and heel to heel, with no gaps. The phrase follows the iqāmah and comes just before the opening takbīr. It rests on the Prophet’s practice of straightening the rows before the prayer. He said that straightening them is part of the perfection of the prayer (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim). The rows express the equality of the worshippers, since rich and poor, young and old stand side by side before God. The wording of the call varies among imams and regions.

title: Istihsan, al-
def: Juristic preference: setting aside an established ruling for a case because another ruling is fairer.
what: Istiḥsān means to hold something to be better. In the law it names the practice of leaving a ruling that strict analogy would give, in favour of another that is more equitable in the particular case. Faruqi describes it as the acceptance of a rule because its equity is superior to that of an already established law. The Hanafi school developed it, and the Maliki school used a close counterpart. Other jurists, among them al-Shafiʿi, objected that it could let personal taste displace the revealed texts. Its defenders replied that it rests on evidence from the sources, such as necessity, custom or the public good, and that it protects the spirit of the law against rigid analogy.
misread: It is sometimes translated “personal preference” or “arbitrary opinion”, while it is a disciplined method that requires a reason grounded in the sources.

title: Istikbar
def: Arrogant power: the excessive and unjust claim to greatness made by tyrants.
what: Istikbār is the noun of istakbara. It names the assumption of excessive power by tyrants, a claim to greatness that no human has. The Quran gives Pharaoh and his armies as the standing example: “He and his hosts were arrogant in the land without right, and thought they would not be returned to Us” (28:39). In Quranic teaching, istikbār goes together with refusing the truth and with oppressing the weak (istiḍʿāf). The powerful who think themselves above accountability stand opposed to those they exploit. Modern Muslim writers sometimes use the word for the arrogant powers of the world that dominate other peoples, in the same sense as the Quran’s account of earlier tyrants.

title: Istiʿmar
def: Mankind’s commission to build up the earth and human society in line with the patterns God revealed to the Prophet.
what: The root of istiʿmār means to inhabit, cultivate and build. The Quran says: “He produced you from the earth and made you settle in it” (11:61), using the verb istaʿmara. Faruqi takes the word in this Quranic sense: the divine commission to reconstruct the material and human world in fulfilment of the patterns that God revealed to His Prophet (peace be upon him). It makes human beings responsible for developing the earth, in farming, building, learning and just social order. The task is part of the trust (amāna) that God gave to humankind. On this view work in the world is a form of obedience when it follows God’s guidance.
misread: In modern Arabic the word means colonialism, which is the opposite of the Quranic sense of building the earth for the good of its people.

title: Istishab, al-
def: Presumption of continuity: an established ruling or state remains in force until evidence shows that it has changed.
what: Istiṣḥāb means keeping something as a companion, and in the law it is the principle that an established rule or condition is presumed to continue unless proof shows that it was revoked or has altered. The default is continuity. Faruqi defines it as the continuation of an established law that is not known to have been revoked or rescinded by any later evidence.

Jurists express the principle in the well-known rule that certainty is not removed by doubt, and they draw support from a hadith in which a man felt something during prayer, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) told him not to leave unless he heard a sound or smelled an odour (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim). Jurists agree on its use in practice, but they differ on how much weight it has as a source.

title: ʿIzzah
def: Might and honour: the high standing that belongs to God, to His Prophet and to the believers.
what: ʿIzza means might, honour and a standing that cannot be overcome. The Quran assigns it first to God: “Whoever desires honour, to God belongs all honour” (35:10). It then names those who share in it by His grant: “Honour belongs to God, to His Messenger and to the believers, but the hypocrites do not know” (63:8). Faruqi lists it as the high position that belongs to God, to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and to the Muslims in their own realms. The same root gives the divine name al-ʿAzīz, the Almighty. Muslims draw on the word to say that the dignity of the community comes from faithfulness to God and does not depend on worldly power.

title: Isma'il Raji al Faruqi
def: Palestinian-American scholar of Islam and comparative religion (1921–1986), professor at Temple University, and a principal source for this site's Glossary.
what: Born in Jaffa, Palestine, in 1921, he studied at the American University of Beirut, took master's degrees in philosophy at Indiana University in 1949 and at Harvard University in 1951, and his doctorate at Indiana in 1952. He then studied Islam in Cairo and Christianity at the Faculty of Divinity of McGill University. He taught at McGill, in Karachi and Cairo, and at Syracuse University, and in 1968 became professor of Islamic studies and history of religions at Temple University in Philadelphia, where he taught until his death.

His work ranged across the study of religion, Islamic thought, ethics, aesthetics and the meeting of faiths, and he set out a new reading of tawḥīd (the unity of God) and its bearing on knowledge. With Fazlur Rahman and Seyyed Hossein Nasr, he was among the most prominent scholars of Islam in North American universities from the 1960s. He and his wife, the scholar Lois Lamya al Faruqi, were murdered in 1986.
sources: The biography follows the front matter of his Islam: Religion, Practice, Culture and World Order, with an introduction by Imtiyaz Yusuf (London and Washington: The International Institute of Islamic Thought, 2012), pp. vii, ix, xi and xv. The terms and Arabic forms in this Glossary follow his Toward Islamic English, and articles on this site cite both works.
